The various sensor outputs are fused with connected vehicle data using artificial intelligence and machine learning located at the specific roadway intersection. These sensing agents of lidar, radar, image processing, stereo cameras, and other technologies are already being used in AV designs, and several initial efforts are deploying these technologies at intersections for enhanced signal control, safety, and traffic management. NLR has been evaluating the early stages of this new generation of traffic control when these sensing and perception agents are incorporated into the roadway infrastructure, with specific attention to the functional benefits of a variety of control applications, as illustrated on the right-hand side of the figure. 36 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. CAV = connected and automated vehicle Source: Stanley Young, National Laboratory of the Rockies IRI planned, deployed, and maintained by the OMA provides an independent safety agent in the AMD network system-of-systems design concept. It augments vehicle-based sensing to help “see around the corner” or other conditions in which any individual vehicle’s sensor stack is occluded. IRI applications can enhance safety by enabling AVs to better match the operating speeds of the general flow of traffic when cooperative driving automation principles using IRI perception and control inform the approaching vehicle of other vehicles, pedestrians, or micromobility users outside their individual field of view. These benefits of IRI, however, do not eliminate the essential requirement for AV fleets to be fully operational in the event that the IRI sensing and communications are interrupted. The AV fleet vehicles must still be capable of safely continuing their fully automated mobility service during situations such as a power outage that disable IRI equipment for a period of time. These IRI “failure mode” conditions may result in lower operating speeds for the AV fleet vehicles within AMD zones normally providing IRI communications. 37 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 4 Summary of Phase III Research This third edition of the AMD implementation report series, which corresponds with NLR’s Phase III of AMD research described herein, provides technical information, data, and critical evaluation of the continuing evolution of the AV industry for public mobility. Phase I and Phase II work drew insights and conclusions primarily from commonalities of the initial 10 early deployment sites, with particular emphasis on ADS performance. However, in Phase III, research began to draw from parallel fields and industries as they relate to the foundational concepts inherent to the design, deployment, and operation of an AMD.
